title: Weekly US Influenza Surveillance Report: Key Updates for Week 35, ending September 5, 2026 - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention | CDC (.gov)

analysis.time: The report covers Week 35, ending September 5, 2026, and was published on September 18, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The surveillance report is for the United States, focusing on national and regional data.
analysis.event: The report indicates that seasonal influenza activity is low during Week 35, ending September 5, 2026. It also notes no new confirmed human infections with a novel influenza virus were reported.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: During Week 35, 1.3% of respiratory specimens tested in clinical laboratories were positive for influenza virus. Influenza A accounted for 93.7% of positive specimens, while Influenza B accounted for 6.3%. No significant risk of widespread transmission was reported.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC is monitoring influenza data through virologic surveillance and is providing interim recommendations for avian influenza A(H5N1) prevention and public health investigations. The data does not reflect specimens tested only at CDC and could include more than one specimen per person.

analysis.brief_en: The CDC's Weekly US Influenza Surveillance Report for Week 35, ending September 5, 2026, indicates low seasonal influenza activity. During this period, 1.3% of respiratory specimens tested in clinical laboratories were positive for influenza, with Influenza A accounting for 93.7% and Influenza B for 6.3%. No new confirmed human infections with a novel influenza virus were reported. The report emphasizes that variant influenza viruses, such as H5N1, have not shown the ability to spread easily and sustainably from person to person. The CDC is monitoring influenza data through virologic surveillance and has issued interim recommendations for avian influenza A(H5N1) prevention and public health investigations. The data reflects specimens tested at public health laboratories and may include multiple specimens per person. The report serves as a key update for understanding influenza trends and is part of broader surveillance efforts that include other respiratory viruses.
